extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, corporate counsel, law students, policymakers, and tech companies evaluating IP strategy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing between patent protection and trade secrecy for inventions, weighing legal standards (subject-matter eligibility, nonobviousness, on-sale bar), costs and timelines, enforceability, and sector-specific considerations (e.g., AI, pharmaceuticals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure vs. nondisclosure tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents require disclosure of the invention in exchange for the right to exclude; trade secrets rely on nondisclosure rather than affirmative disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the fundamental quid pro quo of the patent system (disclosure in exchange for the right to exclude) versus the nondisclosure basis of trade secrecy. Consider whether public disclosure is desirable or necessary for the technology at issue when choosing protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent subject‑matter eligibility (Mayo/Alice framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims must pass the Mayo/Alice two‑step test: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (or other ineligible subject matter), and (2) determine whether the claim contains an inventive concept that transforms the abstract idea into a new and useful process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two‑step test renders patentability of algorithm- and AI-based innovations uncertain; evaluate whether an invention can be framed to survive the Mayo/Alice inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (inventive step) standard and KSR impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be nonobvious (involve an inventive step); KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex broadened the scope of the nonobviousness inquiry and criticized overly rigid tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR warns against limiting the analysis; the USPTO's nonobviousness guidelines reflect KSR's expansive inquiry. Increased nonobviousness scrutiny makes patents more vulnerable to invalidation; assess inventiveness in light of modern, flexible obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with algorithmic/AI innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithm- and AI-based innovations face uncertain patentability under current subject‑matter jurisprudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Mayo/Alice raises questions about abstract ideas and inventive concept, firms working on AI should consider trade secrecy as an alternative or supplemental protection if patents are unlikely to survive eligibility challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent costs and prosecution timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Patenting requires upfront investment and there is a substantial timeline between filing and obtaining a patent (the article cites on average ~20 months to obtain after filing, excluding preparation time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In sectors with rapid technological change and short product life cycles, the time and cost of obtaining a patent may make patents less attractive. Factor expected pendency and prosecution costs into the protection decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret upfront costs and absence of examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrecy requires no initial examination process and generally involves fewer upfront costs compared to patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secrets can be a more flexible and accessible method of guarding proprietary knowledge, particularly for entities seeking to avoid patent prosecution expenses and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy (trade secret maintenance standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secret plaintiffs must demonstrate they made reasonable (i.e., cost‑justified) efforts to maintain secrecy; plaintiffs need not build an 'impenetrable fortress' of secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites E.I. duPont de Nemours & Co. v. Christopher and Judge Posner's Rockwell opinion emphasizing efficiency over maximum security. Courts are wary of encouraging excessive precautions; security measures should be reasonable and cost‑justified rather than absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of protectable subject matter under trade secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrecy covers a broader scope of subject matter than patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because trade secrets are not constrained by statutory patentable subject matter rules, they may protect information that patents cannot; however, enforceability depends on secrecy being maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: No protection against independent invention or reverse engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets provide no remedy when competitors obtain the information through proper means such as independent invention or reverse engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a serious drawback for secrecy-only strategies; where reverse engineering or independent discovery is likely (e.g., many products/processes), patents may be necessary to secure exclusionary rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum and procedural advantages under the DTSA
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA), plaintiffs may choose between state and federal forum and can use supplemental jurisdiction to press state-law misappropriation claims alongside a federal DTSA claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal DTSA remedies and forum choice can make trade secret enforcement more attractive; consider jurisdictional and procedural advantages when evaluating enforcement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pre‑filing secret commercial use/sales (on‑sale bar under AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of products made by a secret process before filing can trigger the on‑sale bar and invalidate later patents; Celanese Int’l Corp. v. Int’l Trade Comm’n (Aug 12, 2024) found the AIA did not change precedent that pre‑filing sales of products made using a secret process block patentability of that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a company commercializes a product made by a secret process more than a year before filing, that activity may foreclose later patenting. Businesses must weigh the risk that secret commercial use may bar subsequent patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector‑specific viability (when patents remain the 'gold standard')
rubrics_metrics.description: In areas where secrecy is not viable—e.g., pharmaceuticals—patents continue to be the gold standard because competitors could otherwise replicate or reformulate the process/product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the nature of the technology makes secrecy impractical (complex products, regulatory disclosures, easy reverse engineering). Where secrecy cannot be realistically maintained, patent protection is often preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for combined use of patents and trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations may implement both patents and trade secrets for competitive advantage; mutual exclusivity between the two is not a given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze which aspects of an innovation to patent and which to keep secret (e.g., patent core inventions, keep manufacturing know‑how secret). Strategic combination can balance disclosure with continued protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and public‑disclosure considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread preference for trade secrecy over patenting could undermine Congress’s policy favoring disclosure; Justice Marshall warned trade secrets may disincentivize patent system participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the societal/public policy implications of choosing secrecy (reduced public disclosure) and whether institutional incentives or legal developments may shift norms or law in response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of monitoring evolving case law and PTO guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent and evolving jurisprudence (e.g., Mayo/Alice, KSR, Celanese) and USPTO guidelines materially affect the relative advantages of patents vs trade secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legal standards shift, businesses should continually reassess IP strategy in light of new court decisions and USPTO policy guidance that alter patentability, obviousness, and enforcement landscapes.
